A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same macaque neural-response modeling study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-response prediction experiments, incremental-training comparisons, architectural ablations and data-efficiency results on two macaques.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds established-model comparisons, alternative-metric evaluations, training controls and preferred-feature analyses.

M1.justification: The CNN architectures, single-head attention, CTL/FCL readouts and incremental freezing procedures remain unchanged in Figures 2–3. The receptive-field description changes from 11×11 to 13×13 pixels without a corresponding architectural revision. Poisson loss appears as an additional experimental control, not a replacement for the proposed method's MSE training.

E1.justification: Primary training and evaluation retain the same M1S1/M2S1 natural-image datasets and 302/299 neurons. v2 Appendix A.2 adds a preferred-feature analysis involving 28 neurons and model responses to artificial pattern stimuli, modestly extending diagnostic stimulus coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares the study's own CNN and attention variants. v2 Appendix A.3/Figure 8 additionally benchmarks ff-CNN against shared-core factorized 'what and where' and goal-driven VGG transfer-learning models. This substantially expands external comparator coverage; transformer models are discussed but explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds CC2_norm, FEV and r2_er evaluations, training controls on 50 M2S1 neurons, and preferred-stimulus analyses. Reported acquisition timing also changes from 1-second stimulus/1-second gray screen to Appendix A.1's 500-ms stimulus/1500-ms blank screen, although Section 3 incorrectly says 1500 seconds. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine preferred features and artificial stimuli (Figure 7), sensitivity to L1 regularization, Poisson loss and dropout removal (Figure 8E), and consistency across evaluation metrics (Figures 9–10). Existing channel-bottleneck, value-mapping, channel-mixing, attention-map and data-efficiency analyses remain, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report SEM and ten repeated presentations of validation stimuli. v2's tabular peak-tuning uncertainties largely replace v1's SEM error bars. No new seed counts, repeated-training protocol, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The correlation entries in Tables 1–2 and data-efficiency Table 3 are retained, while Figures 7–10 add substantial results. For example, v2 reports M2S1 FEV of 0.390 for ff-CNN and 0.408 for ff+sa-CNN. Table 1 reports M1S1 rf-CNN PTS as 1.8, versus approximately 1.5 plotted in v1 Figure 5. Figure 4 also drops the rf+sa-CNN single-neuron example.

T1.justification: The peak-tuning equation and joint/separate ranking definitions remain unchanged. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs, and v2 uses additional established metrics without introducing new mathematical derivations or definitions.

C1.justification: v2 explicitly promotes development of peak-tuning metrics as a contribution in the abstract and evaluation section; v1 already used these metrics without the same explicit novelty claim. The central claims about attention, complementary contextual mechanisms and incremental learning remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains why sparse strong responses can escape FEV and r2_er assessment, emphasizes the zero peak-tuning scores of receptive-field models under reduced data, and connects preferred features to pattern completion. These extend the interpretation while retaining the original center/surround account and gradient-bottleneck hypothesis.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents batch size 50, 50 epochs, coarse hyperparameter selection on 50 neurons, optimization restricted to ff-CNN, receptive-field alignment and the 200–600-ms response-measurement window. These expand existing technical documentation; the optimizer, learning rate, hardware description and code-access link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant work on V1t, shared-core models, pattern completion, recording methods and evaluation metrics. It explicitly distinguishes its mechanistic, single-attention-layer study from transformer-based state-of-the-art prediction. The original related-work framework is largely retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, approach, results and discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Training and evaluation become separate subsections, the initial results sections are consolidated, and appendices are substantially reordered. The title changes, and v1's broader-impacts and ethics paragraph is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adds the preferred-feature, comparator/control and alternative-metric displays in Figures 7–10. It replaces v1's main peak-tuning bar charts with columns in Table 1, enlarges Figure 3, removes one Figure 4 panel and reformats the document. Other original plots are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The established-model comparisons, alternative-metric checks and training controls strengthen the empirical grounding of the existing conclusions, while added setup details improve reproducibility. These benefits are tempered by inconsistent stimulus-timing units and removal of the explicit animal-care approval statement. Overall, the supporting evidence and documentation improve, with some reporting weaknesses remaining.
